claims.text: The high-entropy alloy initially has a uniform, self-forming passive oxide film that provides corrosion protection.
Tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by the interplay between mechanical removal of the passive film and limited rapid film reformation.
Sliding wear intermittently removes the protective passive oxide film.
Removal of the passive film exposes bare substrate to accelerated corrosion under combined mechanical and electrochemical attack.
The integrity and regeneration rate of the passive oxide film mediate the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
Reactive metal sites exposed by film stripping corrode more rapidly than the passivated surface.
Corrosion damage hinders complete reformation of the passive film.
Impaired film reformation creates a feedback loop that further exposes the substrate and synergistically accelerates degradation.
Combined tribo-corrosion will cause greater overall degradation than isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
Combined tribo-corrosion will increase weight loss relative to isolated wear or corrosion.
Combined tribo-corrosion will produce deeper wear tracks relative to isolated wear or corrosion.
Combined tribo-corrosion will produce higher corrosion rates relative to isolated wear or corrosion.
Sufficiently rapid oxide reformation can partially mitigate degradation.
Even when oxide reformation is sufficiently rapid, film removal and delayed repassivation should still elevate overall degradation.
The proposed mechanism should operate when film removal is as fast as or faster than film reformation.
The proposed mechanism may fail when the oxide film reforms extremely rapidly.
The proposed mechanism may fail when wear is so severe that passive-film dynamics no longer significantly govern degradation.
The quantitative contributions of wear and corrosion and the kinetics of film reformation vary with experimental parameters.

contradictions.description: The baseline says the passive film remains largely undisturbed in wear-only and corrosion-only cases, but the hypothesis and mechanism state that mechanical wear strips or disrupts the film. An inert wear-only environment suppresses corrosion but does not by itself prevent mechanical film disruption.

The prediction primarily states that combined degradation exceeds each isolated condition, whereas the falsification rule requires a synergistic increase beyond the additive effects of wear-only plus corrosion-only. Exceeding either isolated control is a weaker criterion than exceeding their sum.
